body.heading: Uggs on Vinted: worth it, but check first
paragraphs: Ugg boots hold their value better than most footwear, and Vinted is full of genuine pairs at a fraction of retail — especially in the run-up to winter, when demand peaks. The classic boots and slippers in popular sizes sell within minutes of being listed.

The catch is that Uggs are counterfeited at a huge scale, and the fakes have got convincing enough that you can't rely on the photos alone. The people who win on Vinted are the ones who know to check the label, the hologram and the sole before they buy.
This guide walks through both sides: what actually sells and what to pay, and how to tell a genuine pair from a fake before you part with your money.

body.heading: How to spot fake Ugg boots
paragraphs: 1. **The security label and QR code.** This is the most reliable check. Since around 2013, genuine Uggs have a sewn-in security label on the left boot with a QR code that scans to Ugg's official site for verification. The label should be stitched in, not a flimsy paper tag — and a crisp holographic element (the sun logo that shifts as you tilt it) is a sign of a genuine pair.

2. **Where they're made.** Genuine Uggs are made in China, Vietnam, Cambodia, the Philippines or the Dominican Republic. If the label says "Made in Australia" or "Made in New Zealand", it's a fake — genuine Uggs have never been made there.
3. **The rebranding tell.** Since 2016, Ugg has dropped the "Australia" from its name — it's just "UGG" now. So any label reading "UGG Australia" is either very old or, more likely, a fake.
4. **The heel label.** Compare the UGG label on the back of the heel against a known-genuine one — fakes often have bigger fonts, poor stitching and off-shade colours.
5. **Sheepskin vs synthetic.** Genuine Uggs use real sheepskin and suede. Fakes use synthetic fur that feels thinner and less dense. If the lining looks flat or shiny in photos, be suspicious.
6. **The sole.** Check the tread pattern and flex against a genuine pair. Fake soles are often harder, with a wrong or shallow tread pattern.
7. **The price.** A brand-new pair of classic Uggs at a fraction of retail is almost always fake. If it's too good to be true, it is.
For the general fake-spotting framework across all brands, see [how to spot fakes on Vinted](/guides/vinted-scams-buyer-protection).

body.heading: What to buy (and what to skip)
paragraphs: Buy the classic boots and slippers in popular sizes — those hold value best and are the most worth an alert. Check the security label photo before you commit, and ask for a close-up of the QR code and the heel label if they're not clear in the listing.

Skip anything without a clear label photo, and be wary of bulk sellers with dozens of "new with tags" Uggs in popular sizes — that's a classic counterfeit pattern. If the seller won't send the label photo, walk away.
For the resale angle, read [how to sell on Vinted](/guides/how-to-sell-on-vinted) — Uggs are a reliable category to source, provided you authenticate every pair first.

body.heading: Why an alert beats refreshing the search
paragraphs: Genuine Uggs in a popular size sell within minutes of being listed, and demand only climbs as winter approaches. If you're checking manually, you're always behind the people who get notified the moment a real pair drops.

A saved-search alert watches for your exact criteria — size, style, price cap — and pings you the instant something matching is listed. You still run the label and sole checks before buying, but you're no longer the last person to see the listing.
[Set up an alert for the Uggs you want](/guides/vinted-price-alert) and you'll catch the genuine pairs before they're gone.

faq.question: Are Ugg boots on Vinted real?
faq.answer: A lot are genuine, but Uggs are heavily counterfeited, so check before you buy. Look for the sewn-in security label with a QR code that scans to Ugg's site, check the boots are made in China/Vietnam/Cambodia/Philippines/Dominican Republic (never Australia or New Zealand), and compare the heel label against a genuine one.

faq.question: How can I spot fake Ugg boots?
faq.answer: Check the security label and QR code first — genuine Uggs have a sewn-in label that scans to Ugg's site, with a crisp holographic sun logo. Then check where they're made (never Australia/NZ), that the label says just 'UGG' not 'UGG Australia', and that the lining is real sheepskin, not synthetic fur.

faq.question: What should I pay for Uggs on Vinted?
faq.answer: It depends on the style, size and condition — classic boots and slippers in popular sizes hold the most value. Check real sold prices rather than asking prices before you buy, so you pay a fair amount. A brand-new pair at a fraction of retail is usually a fake.

faq.question: Should I ask for more photos before buying Uggs on Vinted?
faq.answer: Yes — always ask for a clear photo of the security label, the QR code and the heel label. A genuine seller of a quality pair will send them without fuss; a fake seller will be vague or reuse listing photos. If they won't send close-ups, walk away.

faq.question: Do Uggs hold their value on Vinted?
faq.answer: Yes — classic boots and slippers hold value well, especially in autumn and winter when demand peaks. That's exactly why they're so heavily counterfeited, so authentication is the price of entry for getting a genuine deal.
